summary: Describes Path MTU Discovery for IPv6, largely derived from the IPv4 version in RFC 1191. It lets a sender find the largest packet size that fits the whole path. It replaces RFC 1981.

plainLanguage.summary: Path MTU Discovery helps an IPv6 sender learn the largest packet that can cross every link on a path. Routers report a packet that is too large, and the sender uses that information to send smaller packets.

questions: what is an icmpv6 packet too big message
why is icmpv6 blocking a problem for pmtud
subtitle: How an IPv6 sender learns the largest packet size that can cross a path without fragmentation.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 sender knows the MTU of its first link, but not the smallest MTU on the entire path to its destination.
tldr.mechanism: The sender starts with the first-hop MTU. A node that cannot forward a packet returns an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message with the constricting link's MTU, and the sender lowers its estimate.
tldr.outcome: Path MTU Discovery helps send the largest packets that fit without IPv6 fragmentation. RFC 8201 obsoletes RFC 1981 and notes that blocked ICMPv6 can cause connections to stall.

today: RFC 8201 is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 1981. It is the revised specification for IPv6 Path MTU Discovery.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Packet Size Needs Discovery
sections.content:
The Path MTU (PMTU) is the smallest link MTU along a path between a source and destination. A sender usually wants to use packets no larger than this value, avoiding IPv6 fragmentation where possible.

IPv6 nodes should implement Path MTU Discovery, though a minimal implementation may omit it and use the IPv6 minimum link MTU as its maximum packet size. That can use smaller packets than the path allows. The RFC also describes a failure case: if ICMPv6 messages are blocked, a TCP connection may complete its handshake and then stall when data is sent. This is called a black-hole connection.

RFC 4821 describes Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery for paths where delivery of ICMPv6 messages is not assured.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender needs the smallest packet-size limit across the whole route, not just the first link. If it cannot receive the reports that reveal that limit, data may stop moving even after a connection starts.

sections.title: The Discovery Process
sections.content:
The source initially assumes that the PMTU equals the known MTU of the first-hop link. If a later node cannot forward a packet because it is too large, that node discards it and sends an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message containing the MTU of the constricting link.

The source lowers its PMTU estimate and sends smaller packets. This may repeat if another link further along the path has a smaller MTU. Discovery is complete when the estimate is no greater than the actual PMTU. A node may also stop sending packets larger than the IPv6 minimum link MTU.

Routes can change. Packet Too Big messages reveal decreases; a source can probe occasionally to detect increases. For a multicast destination, the smallest PMTU across the paths in use determines the size of later packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The source starts with the first link's size limit. When a router reports a smaller limit, the source reduces its estimate and sends smaller packets.

sections.title: Rules for Handling Packet Too Big Messages
sections.content:
These requirements apply to nodes that implement Path MTU Discovery. A node should validate that the quoted packet in a Packet Too Big message corresponds to traffic it actually sent.

A message reporting an MTU below the IPv6 minimum link MTU must be discarded, and the PMTU estimate must not fall below that minimum. A valid message lowers the estimate for the relevant path, and the node must reduce packet sizes to avoid repeated drops. It must not increase its estimate based on a Packet Too Big message.

A node may probe for an increase, but it must wait at least 5 minutes after receiving a Packet Too Big message for that path. The recommended timer is 10 minutes. The RFC uses lowercase “must” and “should” and does not apply the RFC 2119 definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: A valid report makes the sender lower its packet-size estimate, but never below IPv6's minimum link MTU. The sender must not treat a Packet Too Big message as proof that the path can carry larger packets.

sections.title: Storing and Refreshing PMTU Information
sections.content:
The implementation notes suggest that the IP layer store PMTU information and that the ICMPv6 layer process Packet Too Big messages. Packetization layers, such as TCP or a protocol built on UDP, can then learn when the maximum send transport-message size changes.

An implementation chooses how to represent a path for its cache. It might keep one PMTU for the whole node, one per destination, or one per flow. A node with multiple interfaces should maintain information for each IPv6 link. The initial value is the first-hop link MTU; a reported value replaces it only when it is lower.

Cached values can become stale. Too-large values are discovered when a packet is dropped, but no event reveals that a value is too small. Implementations should age cached values and probe for a larger PMTU after a period on the order of 10 minutes. The timeout should be configurable.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP layer can keep a size limit for each path and share changes with transport protocols. Because a cached limit may be too small after routes change, implementations should sometimes test for a larger one.

sections.title: What Packetization Layers Do
sections.content:
A packetization layer must use the PMTU for its path and should avoid creating packets larger than that limit, except when probing. A probe packet must not be fragmented to the PMTU. TCP must also respect the Maximum Segment Size (MSS) received from its peer, which reflects the receiver's reassembly limit and is independent of the PMTU.

A Packet Too Big message means a packet was dropped. A reliable upper layer can recover through its normal retransmission method, or may retransmit promptly after notification using a packet no larger than the new PMTU. The layer that retransmits is responsible for congestion control. A loss caused by a PMTU probe must not be treated as a congestion notification.

Some transports cannot split a segment for retransmission. In that case, the IP layer may fragment the original segment when retransmitting it. Later segments should fit within the PMTU.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport protocols should make packets small enough for the path and use their normal recovery when a packet is dropped. A probe loss is a size signal, not by itself a sign of network congestion.

sections.title: Security and Missing ICMPv6 Messages
sections.content:
Forged Packet Too Big messages can cause denial of service. A false report of a very small MTU can reduce performance, but the sender must not lower its estimate below the IPv6 minimum link MTU. A false report of a larger MTU could cause packet loss, but the rules prohibit raising an estimate based on such a message.

Filtering legitimate ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages can prevent the source from learning the actual PMTU and can create a black-hole connection. RFC 4821 describes a discovery method that does not depend on ICMPv6 delivery. RFC 8201 obsoletes RFC 1981 and does not require IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Fake size reports can waste capacity, but the rules limit how far they can mislead the sender. Blocking real Packet Too Big messages can still stop the sender from finding the path limit.
